title: What isn't of it
hook: whoever introduces into this matter of ours what isn't of it, it is rejected
tomorrow: between the allowed and the forbidden is a gray zone. then what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, written in the womb: four things written before a first breath, and the companions told to act anyway. Written, and still we strive. Today, the striving gets a boundary.

Every family has a recipe that isn't up for discussion. A cousin adds something new to it, and honestly, it's good, and the kitchen still goes quiet. Good, sure. But that's not the recipe. Yesterday's question: can you add something beautiful to the religion? Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports his answer, and it's short. Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what isn't of it, it is rejected.
screen: `NOT UP FOR DISCUSSION.` → `GOOD, BUT NOT THE RECIPE.` → `WHAT ISN'T OF IT IS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: The word for that kind of addition is bid'ah, something newly invented. Everything turns on one phrase: this matter of ours. Commentators read it as the religion itself, its worship and its rulings, what counts as drawing near to Allah. So this isn't a hadith against new things. A new way to teach, a new building, a new tool are outside its reach. What it rejects is a new act of worship, a new ritual, a new 'this is what Allah wants' that was never taught. And the word for rejected is radd, which also means sent back, returned to the sender. Sahih Muslim's wording widens it from inventing to doing: whoever does a deed that isn't in line with our matter, it is rejected. Why so firm about something meant kindly? Because worship is a reply to what was given, and once additions pile up, nobody can tell the original from the extras. Scholars differ at the edges. Some sort new things into praiseworthy and blameworthy, and call only the blameworthy kind the bid'ah of this hadith. Others say nothing added to worship is ever praiseworthy, and a good new tool just isn't bid'ah at all. Both keep the center: the worship stays as it came.
screen: `BID'AH: NEWLY INVENTED.` · `'THIS MATTER OF OURS': THE RELIGION.` · `RADD: SENT BACK.` · `SCHOLARS DIFFER AT THE EDGES.` · then, large: `KEEP IT AS IT CAME.`

segments.voice: Choose one practice you already keep: a prayer, a blessing before food, the way your family greets a guest. Ask where you learned it, and whether anything has drifted along the way. Then plan one moment this week to do it exactly as it was taught: when, where, and the one thing most likely to get in the way.
screen: `ONE PRACTICE YOU KEEP.` · `HAS IT DRIFTED?` · `WHEN, WHERE, WHAT'S IN THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Bid'ah: something newly invented, and in this hadith, an addition to the religion itself. It's sent back, radd, however beautiful it looked.
Your line: keep it as it came, the worship as taught and the rest of life open to good ideas. That's one week of the last range.

screen: `DAY 1433 COUNTS.` → `YEAR FIVE · 7 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: BETWEEN THE ALLOWED AND THE FORBIDDEN IS A GRAY ZONE. THEN WHAT?`

howItsDone: Muslims learn acts of worship, such as the prayer, the washing before it and the words said in it, from the Qur'an and the sunnah through teachers, and take care to keep them as they were taught.

fork.setup: an uncle makes up a special line to say before family meals and tells the kids it's 'the sunnah way.' what does today's hadith speak to?
options: calling his own line the Prophet's way: that adds to the religion.
eating together at all: any new family custom at meals is rejected.
nothing: his intention is good, so whatever he adds is fine.
fork.reveal: the hadith is about 'this matter of ours': presenting something as worship or sunnah when it wasn't taught. a family meal isn't the problem.

chat.says: made a sticker chart for kids who pray on time. one parent texted me 'bid'ah'. is it??
options: A chart helps them learn; it isn't a new act of worship. Keep the prayer as taught.
Yes. Anything new tied to religion gets rejected, so take the chart down.
No. Any addition is fine, honestly, as long as your intention is good.
chat.meaning: The hadith rejects additions to the religion itself. A teaching aid adds nothing to the prayer, which stays exactly as it came.

bid'ah.meaning: something newly invented; here, an addition to the religion

Aisha.meaning: a wife of the Prophet, who reported this hadith

Sahih Muslim.meaning: a major collection of hadith, gathered by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
